rv.q: We’re always entertained, frequently laughing — at the same time, as in certain Wes Anderson movies, there’s something in the extra-stylish surface that keeps deeper feelings at bay.

The play Reddick has built on the foundation of that experience, Cold War Choir Practice, is a coming-of-age fantasia that embraces a wild array of genres and styles, leading us down a path filled with farce, music, and suspense to some stark truths that ring as true now as they did in the play’s 1987 setting: Institutional power can steamroller...
Adams brings Ro Reddick's exhilarating 'Cold War Choir Practice' to perverse life at MCC Theater.
This spirit of trust and integrity to the world of the play makes Cold War Choir Practice soar.
Reddick's writing retains a sense of play, allowing humor and absurdity to coexist with the darker implications of the story.

This is a surprise and a disappointment, because so much of “Cold War Choir Practice” is so good, not least its first-rate cast led by Alana Raquel Bowers, an adult who is completely convincing as ten-year-old Meek.

So much of what busily precedes and follows this as Meek ruminates, brothers Smooch and Clay confront each other, Puddin complains and accuses, and Virgie’s frame of mind devolves doesn’t seem to make cohesive sense.
Adams proves, once again, his deft ability to sculpt wildly dense material, assembling a first-rate acting company that knows exactly what world they're living in.

rv.cn: The Recs RDC - Randall David Cook
rv.q: Nothing cold about this red-hot show that is not to be missed.
That's not to say that there aren't things to enjoy in Reddick's play... Or that there aren't similar pleasures to be found in the supple staging by Knud Adams.

cn.t: Critics largely praise Reddick's inventive, absurdist take on Cold War anxieties through a child's eyes, with standout performances and bold direction, though some find the tonal shifts from comedy to espionage jarring and overly cute.
